questions.stem: Which three parameters classify every English consonant?
questions.explanation: The three-term system: place (where), manner (how), voicing (vocal fold vibration or not).

questions.stem: How many consonant phonemes does English have according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture applies the classification to all twenty-four consonant phonemes of English.

questions.stem: Match the place of articulation to the articulators involved:
options: Labiodental — lower lip and upper teeth
Velar — tongue back and soft palate
questions.explanation: Dental = tongue and upper teeth; tongue + alveolar ridge = alveolar.

questions.stem: Match the manner of articulation to its description:
options: Fricative — a narrow gap that creates audible friction
Approximant — complete closure with air through the nose
Affricate — a plosive closure with a fricative release
Plosive — complete closure followed by a sudden release
questions.explanation: Approximants involve only a slight narrowing with no audible friction; air through the nose (lowered velum) defines nasals.

questions.stem: Which are voiceless/voiced pairs sharing the same place and manner?
questions.explanation: Pairs: /p/–/b/, /t/–/d/, /k/–/g/, /f/–/v/, /s/–/z/, /θ/–/ð/. /m/ and /n/ differ in place (bilabial vs alveolar).

questions.stem: In the lecture's consonant chart, when two symbols share a cell:
options: They differ in manner of articulation
The left one is voiceless and the right one is voiced
The left one is voiced and the right one is voiceless
They differ in place of articulation
questions.explanation: Symbols in the same cell share place and manner; left = voiceless, right = voiced.
/ʃ/ = voiceless post-alveolar fricative. The affricates are /tʃ/ and /dʒ/.
Its voiceless partner /tʃ/ is in "chest". The palatal approximant is /j/ (yawn).

questions.stem: Which consonant–word pairs from the lecture are correct?
questions.explanation: The same spelling "th" is voiceless /θ/ in thorax and voiced /ð/ in this.

questions.stem: Which consonants are approximants according to the lecture's table?
questions.explanation: /h/ is a voiceless glottal fricative. /r/ is a post-alveolar approximant.

questions.stem: Which IPA transcriptions match the lecture?
Which sound is a glottal fricative?
questions.explanation: Glottal = produced at the vocal folds themselves; /h/ is the voiceless glottal fricative.

questions.stem: How many places of articulation does the lecture list for English consonants?
questions.explanation: Bilabial, labiodental, dental, alveolar, post-alveolar, palatal, velar, glottal.
